intro: Paderewski played Chopin’s Waltz in C♯ minor, Op. 64 No. 2, in this 1917 recording. He was a strong advocate of rubato, the freedom to stretch and quicken a phrase, and Chopin’s score already requires the pianist to move between three different tempos.

sections.label: A · Tempo giusto theme in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: Tempo giusto over a bass note and two chords.

sections.label: B · Più mosso, quicker descending tune
sections.mNote: Più mosso; the right hand plays running figures.

sections.label: C · D♭ major, more slowly
sections.mNote: Più lento. A long melody alternating with notes in an inner voice.

sections.label: D · Quavers and opening melody, C♯ minor
sections.mNote: C♯ minor returns with the two earlier tunes.

sections.label: E · The last Più mosso
sections.mNote: The descending tune returns to close the waltz.

cues.title: Opening, right hand in two voices
cues.text: Chopin’s opening instruction is Tempo giusto. The right hand begins in two voices, with long notes that carry over the bar line before a quick flourish follows. In each bar the left hand plays a bass note and two chords.
cues.evidence: Waltz score, opening Tempo giusto; Knute Snortum engraving (2023), p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paderewski on rubato, 1909
cues.text: In his 1909 essay, Paderewski called rubato “this irreconcilable foe of the metronome”. He rejected the idea that every moment borrowed by slowing must be paid back by speeding up. For a solo pianist, he wrote, “What is lost is lost.”
cues.evidence: Paderewski, ‘Tempo Rubato’, written for Henry T. Finck’s Success in Music and How It Is Won (1909), chapter 28, pp. 454–61. https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol4no1/paderewski-tempo-rubato/

cues.title: The Più mosso refrain
cues.text: Chopin built the waltz around the running Più mosso tune. It appears three times, after the opening melody, after the D♭ major section and again at the end. The score’s sequence is Tempo giusto, Più mosso, Più lento, Più mosso, Tempo primo, Più mosso.
cues.evidence: The score’s complete sequence is Tempo giusto, Più mosso, Più lento, Più mosso, Tempo primo, Più mosso. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Final Più mosso
cues.text: The final Più mosso sets six running quavers in the right hand above three beats in the left. The melody falls in slurred arcs, then climbs to a high note and starts again. Its last descent ends in C♯ minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
